claim: ANAC044 and ANAC085 are NAC-type transcription factors required for DNA damage-induced G2 arrest in Arabidopsis.
source: Here we report that in Arabidopsis, the NAC-type transcription factors ANAC044 and ANAC085 are required for DNA damage-induced G2 arrest.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Under genotoxic stress conditions, ANAC044 and ANAC085 enhance protein accumulation of the R1R2R3-type Myb transcription factor (Rep-MYB).
source: Under genotoxic stress conditions, ANAC044 and ANAC085 enhance protein accumulation of the R1R2R3-type Myb transcription factor (Rep-MYB), which represses G2/M-specific genes.
evidence: The abstract states this mechanism directly, supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Rep-MYB represses G2/M-specific genes.
source: Under genotoxic stress conditions, ANAC044 and ANAC085 enhance protein accumulation of the R1R2R3-type Myb transcription factor (Rep-MYB), which represses G2/M-specific genes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the function of Rep-MYB in repressing G2/M-specific genes.

claim: ANAC044/ANAC085-dependent accumulation of Rep-MYB and cell cycle arrest are observed in the response to heat stress that causes G2 arrest.
source: ANAC044/ANAC085-dependent accumulation of Rep-MYB and cell cycle arrest are also observed in the response to heat stress that causes G2 arrest, but not to osmotic stress that retards G1 progression.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding about heat stress response.

claim: ANAC044/ANAC085-dependent accumulation of Rep-MYB and cell cycle arrest are not observed in response to osmotic stress that retards G1 progression.
source: ANAC044/ANAC085-dependent accumulation of Rep-MYB and cell cycle arrest are also observed in the response to heat stress that causes G2 arrest, but not to osmotic stress that retards G1 progression.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that osmotic stress does not involve ANAC044/ANAC085-dependent mechanisms.

claim: Plants deploy the ANAC044/ANAC085-mediated signalling module as a hub which perceives distinct stress signals and leads to G2 arrest.
source: These results suggest that plants deploy the ANAC044/ANAC085-mediated signalling module as a hub which perceives distinct stress signals and leads to G2 arrest.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this interpretation of the results.

claim: Cell cycle arrest is an active response to stresses that enables organisms to survive under fluctuating environmental conditions.
source: Cell cycle arrest is an active response to stresses that enables organisms to survive under fluctuating environmental conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background knowledge.

claim: The putative core module orchestrating cell cycle arrest in response to various stresses is still elusive.
source: While signalling pathways that inhibit cell cycle progression have been elucidated, the putative core module orchestrating cell cycle arrest in response to various stresses is still elusive.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the knowledge gap the study addresses.

claim: In animals, failure to adapt against disadvantageous stresses leads to various diseases such as cancer.
source: In animals, failure to adapt against disadvantageous stresses leads to various diseases such as cancer, and, in severe cases, cells perish (Twayana and Ravanan, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Twayana and Ravanan, 2018.

claim: The high osmolarity glycerol (HOG) MAP kinase (MAPK) cascade induces cell cycle arrest by inhibiting the transcription of cyclin genes in response to hyperosmotic stress.
source: For instance, the high osmolarity glycerol (HOG) MAP kinase (MAPK) cascade induces cell cycle arrest by inhibiting the transcription of cyclin genes in response to hyperosmotic stress (Saito and Posas, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Saito and Posas, 2012.

claim: Various transcription factors that respond to abiotic stresses have been well studied in plants, including those belonging to the MYB, bZIP, DREB and DREB1s/CBF families.
source: Various transcription factors that respond to abiotic stresses have been well studied, such as those belonging to the MYB, bZIP, drought-responsive element-binding protein (DREB) and DREB1s/C-repeat binding factor (CBF) families (Vinocur and Altman, 2005; Umezawa et al., 2006; Golldack et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Downstream signalling pathways that inhibit cell proliferation in plants remain largely unknown.
source: However, downstream signalling pathways that inhibit cell proliferation remain largely unknown; therefore, it remains to be established whether plants deploy central signalling pathway(s) that induce cell cycle arrest upon exposure to multiple stresses.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: DNA damage arrests the cell cycle to allow DNA repair to occur before DNA replication or mitosis begins.
source: DNA damage also arrests the cell cycle to allow DNA repair to occur before DNA replication or mitosis begins (Harper and Elledge, 2007; Ciccia and Elledge, 2010; Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: DNA damage is sensed by two kinases, ATAXIA TELANGIECTASIA MUTATED (ATM) and ATM AND RAD3-RELATED (ATR).
source: DNA damage is sensed by two kinases, ATAXIA TELANGIECTASIA MUTATED (ATM) and ATM AND RAD3-RELATED (ATR) (Abraham, 2001; Garcia et al., 2003; Culligan et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: ATM is activated by double-strand breaks (DSBs).
source: ATM is activated by double-strand breaks (DSBs), whereas ATR senses single-strand breaks (SSBs) and stalled replication forks (Bensimon et al., 2011; Flynn and Zou, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: ATR senses single-strand breaks (SSBs) and stalled replication forks.
source: ATM is activated by double-strand breaks (DSBs), whereas ATR senses single-strand breaks (SSBs) and stalled replication forks (Bensimon et al., 2011; Flynn and Zou, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: In animals, ATM phosphorylates the checkpoint kinase CHK2, which stabilizes the transcription factor p53 and induces expression of the CDK inhibitor p21, resulting in cell cycle arrest at G1/S phase.
source: In animals, ATM phosphorylates the checkpoint kinase CHK2, which stabilizes the transcription factor p53 and induces expression of the CDK inhibitor p21, resulting in cell cycle arrest at G1/S phase (Donjerkovic and Scott, 2000; Bartek and Lukas, 2001; Cheng and Chen, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: CHK1, which is phosphorylated by ATR, and CHK2 activate the G2/M-phase checkpoint by phosphorylating CDC25 phosphatases.
source: CHK1, which is phosphorylated by ATR, and CHK2 also activate the G2/M-phase checkpoint by phosphorylating CDC25 phosphatases (Karlsson-Rosenthal and Millar, 2006; Perry and Kornbluth, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Plants possess ATM and ATR but lack functional orthologues for p21, p53, CDC25 or CHK1/2.
source: In contrast, while plants possess ATM and ATR, they lack functional orthologues for p21, p53, CDC25 or CHK1/2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about plant DNA damage response.

claim: SOG1 is a plant-specific NAC-type transcription factor that is phosphorylated and activated by ATM and ATR, and triggers DNA damage responses (DDRs).
source: Instead, a plant-specific NAC-type transcription factor, SUPPRESSOR OF GAMMA RESPONSE 1 (SOG1), is phosphorylated and activated by ATM and ATR, and triggers DNA damage responses (DDRs) (Yoshiyama et al., 2009; Yoshiyama et al., 2013; Sjogren et al., 2015; Yoshiyama et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: SOG1 regulates the expression of almost all genes induced by DSBs in Arabidopsis.
source: A previous study demonstrated that in Arabidopsis, SOG1 regulates the expression of almost all genes induced by DSBs (Yoshiyama et al., 2009), causes G2 arrest in the meristem, enhances the transition from cell division to endoreplication (a repeated cycle of DNA replication without mitosis), and triggers stem cell death (Furukawa et al., 2010; Adachi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yoshiyama et al., 2009.

claim: SOG1 causes G2 arrest in the meristem.
source: A previous study demonstrated that in Arabidopsis, SOG1 regulates the expression of almost all genes induced by DSBs (Yoshiyama et al., 2009), causes G2 arrest in the meristem, enhances the transition from cell division to endoreplication (a repeated cycle of DNA replication without mitosis), and triggers stem cell death (Furukawa et al., 2010; Adachi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Furukawa et al., 2010 and Adachi et al., 2011.

claim: SOG1 enhances the transition from cell division to endoreplication.
source: A previous study demonstrated that in Arabidopsis, SOG1 regulates the expression of almost all genes induced by DSBs (Yoshiyama et al., 2009), causes G2 arrest in the meristem, enhances the transition from cell division to endoreplication (a repeated cycle of DNA replication without mitosis), and triggers stem cell death (Furukawa et al., 2010; Adachi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Furukawa et al., 2010 and Adachi et al., 2011.

claim: SOG1 triggers stem cell death.
source: A previous study demonstrated that in Arabidopsis, SOG1 regulates the expression of almost all genes induced by DSBs (Yoshiyama et al., 2009), causes G2 arrest in the meristem, enhances the transition from cell division to endoreplication (a repeated cycle of DNA replication without mitosis), and triggers stem cell death (Furukawa et al., 2010; Adachi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Furukawa et al., 2010 and Adachi et al., 2011.

claim: Expression of CDK inhibitors, such as SMR5 and SMR7, is directly induced by SOG1.
source: Expression of CDK inhibitors, such as SMR5 and SMR7, is directly induced by SOG1 (Yin et al., 2014; Ogita et al., 2018); however, their induction also occurs in DSB-tolerant Arabidopsis mutants, suggesting that it is not sufficient to arrest the cell cycle (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Yin et al., 2014 and Ogita et al., 2018.

claim: Induction of SMR5 and SMR7 is not sufficient to arrest the cell cycle.
source: Expression of CDK inhibitors, such as SMR5 and SMR7, is directly induced by SOG1 (Yin et al., 2014; Ogita et al., 2018); however, their induction also occurs in DSB-tolerant Arabidopsis mutants, suggesting that it is not sufficient to arrest the cell cycle (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: Simultaneous suppression of a set of G2/M-specific genes is accompanied by DNA damage-induced G2 arrest.
source: We previously demonstrated that simultaneous suppression of a set of G2/M-specific genes is accompanied by DNA damage-induced G2 arrest (Adachi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Adachi et al., 2011.

claim: G2/M-specific genes are controlled by three Myb repeat-containing transcription factors, called R1R2R3-Myb or MYB3R.
source: G2/M-specific genes, such as those encoding mitotic cyclins, are controlled by three Myb repeat-containing transcription factors, called R1R2R3-Myb or MYB3R (Ito, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ito, 2005.

claim: Arabidopsis possesses five genes for MYB3R, MYB3R1 to MYB3R5.
source: Arabidopsis possesses five genes for MYB3R, MYB3R1 to MYB3R5, among which MYB3R4 acts as a transcriptional activator (Act-MYB), and MYB3R3 and MYB3R5 are transcriptional repressors (Rep-MYB) (Haga et al., 2007; Haga et al., 2011; Kobayashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: MYB3R4 acts as a transcriptional activator (Act-MYB).
source: Arabidopsis possesses five genes for MYB3R, MYB3R1 to MYB3R5, among which MYB3R4 acts as a transcriptional activator (Act-MYB), and MYB3R3 and MYB3R5 are transcriptional repressors (Rep-MYB) (Haga et al., 2007; Haga et al., 2011; Kobayashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: MYB3R3 and MYB3R5 are transcriptional repressors (Rep-MYB).
source: Arabidopsis possesses five genes for MYB3R, MYB3R1 to MYB3R5, among which MYB3R4 acts as a transcriptional activator (Act-MYB), and MYB3R3 and MYB3R5 are transcriptional repressors (Rep-MYB) (Haga et al., 2007; Haga et al., 2011; Kobayashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: MYB3R1 functions as both an activator and a repressor.
source: MYB3R1 functions as both an activator and a repressor (Kobayashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kobayashi et al., 2015.

claim: MYB3Rs bind to target gene promoters via a cis-acting element called the mitosis-specific activator (MSA) element.
source: MYB3Rs bind to target gene promoters via a cis-acting element called the mitosis-specific activator (MSA) element, and control the expression of G2/M-specific genes (Kobayashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kobayashi et al., 2015.

claim: Rep-MYBs are actively degraded via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, but become stabilized under DNA damage conditions.
source: We recently reported that Rep-MYBs are actively degraded via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, but become stabilized under DNA damage conditions, thereby suppressing G2/M-specific genes and causing G2 arrest (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: Protein stability of Rep-MYBs is dependent on CDK activity.
source: Protein stability of Rep-MYBs is dependent on CDK activity: CDK phosphorylates the C-terminal domain of MYB3R3/5 and promotes their degradation.
evidence: This statement is supported by the context and citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: CDK phosphorylates the C-terminal domain of MYB3R3/5 and promotes their degradation.
source: Protein stability of Rep-MYBs is dependent on CDK activity: CDK phosphorylates the C-terminal domain of MYB3R3/5 and promotes their degradation.
evidence: This statement is supported by the context and citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: DNA damage phosphorylates and activates SOG1, and reduces CDK activities, probably by inducing CDK inhibitor genes, thereby stabilizing Rep-MYBs.
source: Therefore, we proposed a model in which DNA damage phosphorylates and activates SOG1, and reduces CDK activities, probably by inducing CDK inhibitor genes, thereby stabilizing Rep-MYBs (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: Rep-MYBs function as major repressors of cell cycle genes in the response to DNA damage.
source: A recent report also demonstrated that Rep-MYBs function as major repressors of cell cycle genes in the response to DNA damage (Bourbousse et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bourbousse et al., 2018.

claim: ANAC044 and ANAC085 are the closest relatives of SOG1 among NAC transcription factors.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of NAC transcription factors indicated that ANAC044 and ANAC085 are the closest relatives of SOG1 (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing the phylogenetic tree.

claim: In the NAC domain, the amino acid similarity of ANAC044 to SOG1 is 72.0%.
source: indeed, in the NAC domain, which is essential for DNA binding, their amino acid similarity to SOG1 is 72.0% for ANAC044 and 72.6% for ANAC085.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a quantitative measure of similarity.

claim: In the NAC domain, the amino acid similarity of ANAC085 to SOG1 is 72.6%.
source: indeed, in the NAC domain, which is essential for DNA binding, their amino acid similarity to SOG1 is 72.0% for ANAC044 and 72.6% for ANAC085.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a quantitative measure of similarity.

claim: The C-terminal regions carrying the domain needed for transcriptional regulation are shorter in ANAC044 and ANAC085 than in SOG1.
source: A striking difference is that the C-terminal regions carrying the domain needed for transcriptional regulation are shorter in ANAC044 and ANAC085 than in SOG1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed in Figure 1B.

claim: Five serine-glutamine (SQ) motifs, which are targets for phosphorylation by ATM and ATR, are present towards the C terminus of SOG1, but missing in ANAC044 and ANAC085.
source: Moreover, five serine-glutamine (SQ) motifs, which are targets for phosphorylation by ATM and ATR, are present towards the C terminus of SOG1, but missing in ANAC044 and ANAC085 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The transcript levels of ANAC044 and ANAC085 increased soon after bleomycin treatment and reached maxima after 12 hr.
source: The transcript levels of ANAC044 and ANAC085 increased soon after bleomycin treatment and reached maxima after 12 hr, indicating a rapid response to DSBs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GUS expression driven by the ANAC044 promoter was elevated by bleomycin treatment in root tips and young leaves.
source: On the other hand, in the ProANAC044:GUS line, GUS expression was elevated by bleomycin treatment in root tips and young leaves (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: A patchy pattern of GUS signals was observed in the root tip of ProANAC044:GUS plants treated with bleomycin, suggesting that ANAC044 is induced in cells at particular cell cycle stage(s) that are more sensitive to DSBs.
source: Interestingly, we observed a patchy pattern of signals in the root tip, suggesting that ANAC044 is induced in cells at particular cell cycle stage(s) that are more sensitive to DSBs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed GUS staining pattern.

claim: Treatment with hydroxyurea (HU), mitomycin C (MMC), and methyl methanesulfonate (MMS) induced GUS expression in root tips and young leaves of ProANAC044:GUS plants.
source: We also tested other DNA-damaging agents, namely hydroxyurea (HU), mitomycin C (MMC) and methyl methanesulfonate (MMS). HU inhibits deoxyribonucleotide production, thereby causing DNA replication stress (Wang and Liu, 2006; Saban and Bujak, 2009). MMS is an alkylating agent that methylates guanine and adenine bases, resulting in base mispairing and replication blocks (Beranek, 1990; Llorente et al., 2008). MMC generates interstrand cross-links on DNA (Rink et al., 1996). Treatment with all three drugs again induced GUS expression in root tips and young leaves (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C), suggesting that ANAC044 is associated with the DDR in actively dividing cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Bleomycin-induced expression of ANAC044 and ANAC085 was not observed in sog1-101.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, bleomycin-induced expression of ANAC044 and ANAC085 was not observed in sog1-101.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SOG1 is required for the transcriptional induction of ANAC044 and ANAC085 in response to bleomycin.
source: A similar result was also obtained using the ProANAC044:GUS reporter gene, which did not show bleomycin-triggered GUS expression in the sog1-101 mutant background (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), indicating that SOG1 is required for the transcriptional induction.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The promoters of ANAC044 and ANAC085 contain SOG1-binding motifs.
source: We searched for the SOG1-binding motif CTT(N)7AAG in the promoter regions of ANAC044 and ANAC085, and found CTTGGGGAGCAAG and CTTATTTACGAAG sequences, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: SOG1 binds to the ANAC044 and ANAC085 promoters under DNA damage conditions.
source: The result showed that for both ANAC044 and ANAC085, the promoter regions containing the SOG1-binding motifs were highly enriched when chromatin isolated from bleomycin-treated plants, but not from non-treated control, was used for immunoprecipitation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C). This strongly suggests that SOG1 binds to the ANAC044 and ANAC085 promoters under DNA damage conditions and induces their expression.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: anac044-1 and anac044-2 have T-DNA insertions in the fourth and fifth exons of ANAC044, respectively.
source: anac044-1 (SAIL_1286D02) and anac044-2 (GABI_968B05) have T-DNA insertions in the fourth and fifth exons of ANAC044, respectively, and anac085-1 (GABI_894G04) and anac085-2 (SALK_208662) contain T-DNA fragments in the fourth exon of ANAC085 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: anac085-1 and anac085-2 contain T-DNA fragments in the fourth exon of ANAC085.
source: anac044-1 (SAIL_1286D02) and anac044-2 (GABI_968B05) have T-DNA insertions in the fourth and fifth exons of ANAC044, respectively, and anac085-1 (GABI_894G04) and anac085-2 (SALK_208662) contain T-DNA fragments in the fourth exon of ANAC085 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: anac044-1, anac044-2, anac085-1, and anac085-2 are null alleles.
source: Semi-quantitative RT-PCR showed that transcripts of ANAC044 in anac044-1 and anac044-2, and ANAC085 in anac085-1 and anac085-2, were undetectable using primers flanking the T-DNA insertion sites, indicating that all are null alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: anac044 and anac085 mutants were more tolerant than WT to bleomycin, HU, MMC, and MMS.
source: Measurement of root growth showed that the two mutants for each of anac044 or anac085 were more tolerant than WT to all four DNA-damaging agents, and that root growth was almost the same between anac044 and anac085 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The anac044-1 anac085-1 double mutant showed a similar tolerance to DNA-damaging agents as the single mutants.
source: Moreover, the anac044-1 anac085-1 double mutant showed a similar tolerance to that of the single mutants (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The tolerance to bleomycin and MMS was comparable between sog1-101, anac044-1 anac085-1 and the triple mutant anac044-1 anac085-1 sog1-101.
source: We found that the tolerance to bleomycin and MMS was comparable between sog1-101, anac044-1 anac085-1 and the triple mutant anac044-1 anac085-1 sog1-101 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The triple mutant anac044-1 anac085-1 sog1-101 exhibited hypersensitivity to HU and MMC to a similar extent to that of sog1-101.
source: Moreover, the triple mutant exhibited hypersensitivity to HU and MMC to a similar extent to that of sog1-101 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), indicating that sog1-101 is epistatic to anac044-1 anac085-1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: sog1-101 is epistatic to anac044-1 anac085-1.
source: Moreover, the triple mutant exhibited hypersensitivity to HU and MMC to a similar extent to that of sog1-101 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), indicating that sog1-101 is epistatic to anac044-1 anac085-1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the genetic data.

claim: ANAC044 and ANAC085 function downstream of SOG1 in DNA damage-induced root growth retardation.
source: These results suggest that ANAC044 and ANAC085 function downstream of SOG1 in DNA damage-induced root growth retardation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the epistasis data.

claim: DSBs induce cell death of stem cells and stele precursor cells in the root tip.
source: It was reported that DSBs induce cell death of stem cells and stele precursor cells in the root tip, and that SOG1 is involved in this response (Furukawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Furukawa et al., 2010.

claim: SOG1 is involved in DSB-induced stem cell death.
source: It was reported that DSBs induce cell death of stem cells and stele precursor cells in the root tip, and that SOG1 is involved in this response (Furukawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Furukawa et al., 2010.

claim: Almost no cell death was observed in anac044-1 anac085-1, sog1-101 or anac044-1 anac085-1 sog1-101 after bleomycin treatment.
source: Propidium iodide (PI)-stained dead cells were visible in the stem cell and stele precursor cell populations in WT, while almost no cell death was observed in anac044-1 anac085-1, sog1-101 or anac044-1 anac085-1 sog1-101 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A and B.

claim: ANAC044 and ANAC085 participate in SOG1-mediated induction of stem cell death.
source: This result suggests that ANAC044 and ANAC085 also participate in SOG1-mediated induction of stem cell death.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cell death data.

claim: The stem cell niche in Arabidopsis roots is regenerated through experiencing cell death after an acute dose of ionizing radiation (150 Gy).
source: Johnson et al. (2018) investigated the recovery of Arabidopsis roots after an acute dose of ionizing radiation (150 Gy). They found that the stem cell niche was regenerated through experiencing cell death, and that root growth recovered after about one week.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Johnson et al., 2018.

claim: The sog1 mutant underwent neither death nor regeneration of stem cells after ionizing radiation, leading to root growth arrest after long-term culture.
source: However, the sog1 mutant underwent neither death nor regeneration of stem cells, leading to root growth arrest after long-term culture (Johnson et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Johnson et al., 2018.

claim: SOG1-dependent programmed cell death triggers regeneration of the stem cell niche, and is essential for the recovery of root growth.
source: This observation suggests that SOG1-dependent programmed cell death triggers regeneration of the stem cell niche, and is thus essential for the recovery of root growth.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data from Johnson et al., 2018.

claim: In WT roots, PI-stained dead cells derived from stem cells and stele precursor cells gradually decreased and almost disappeared within five days after bleomycin treatment.
source: In WT roots, PI-stained dead cells derived from stem cells and stele precursor cells gradually decreased and almost disappeared within five days (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: In sog1-101, stem cell death did not occur after bleomycin treatment, although sporadic cell death across the meristematic zone and distorted tissue organization were observed.
source: In sog1-101, stem cell death did not occur, although we observed sporadic cell death across the meristematic zone and distorted tissue organization (Figure 3C), which were also described by Johnson et al. (2018).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: anac044-1 anac085-1 displayed no cell death in the stem cell niche or in the meristematic zone, and cells were properly arranged in the root tip throughout 7 days after recovery from bleomycin treatment.
source: On the other hand, anac044-1 anac085-1 displayed no cell death in the stem cell niche or in the meristematic zone, and cells were properly arranged in the root tip throughout 7 days after recovery (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: The anac044-1 anac085-1 sog1-101 triple mutant showed disorganized root tissues as observed in sog1-101.
source: The anac044-1 anac085-1 sog1-101 triple mutant showed disorganized root tissues as observed in sog1-101 (Figure 3C), again indicating epistasis of sog1-101 over anac044-1 anac085-1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: DNA-damaged stem cells in anac044-1 anac085-1, but not sog1-101, can function in producing transit-amplifying cells, which constitute the root meristem.
source: These results suggest that stem cells in sog1-101 and anac044-1 anac085-1 have different characteristics; namely, DNA-damaged stem cells in anac044-1 anac085-1, but not sog1-101, can function in producing transit-amplifying cells, which constitute the root meristem.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the recovery data.

claim: SOG1-dependent, but ANAC044/085-independent, pathway(s) are probably required for preserving the integrity of stem cells that have been exposed to DNA damage.
source: SOG1-dependent, but ANAC044/085-independent, pathway(s) are probably required for preserving the integrity of stem cells that have been exposed to DNA damage.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: DNA repair and recombination are induced through SOG1 in response to DSBs in Arabidopsis.
source: In Arabidopsis, DNA repair and recombination are known to be induced through SOG1 in response to DSBs (Yoshiyama et al., 2009); indeed, our recent study showed that SOG1 directly controls several DNA repair-related genes, such as RAD51 and BRCA1 (Ogita et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Yoshiyama et al., 2009 and Ogita et al., 2018.

claim: SOG1 directly controls several DNA repair-related genes, such as RAD51 and BRCA1.
source: In Arabidopsis, DNA repair and recombination are known to be induced through SOG1 in response to DSBs (Yoshiyama et al., 2009); indeed, our recent study showed that SOG1 directly controls several DNA repair-related genes, such as RAD51 and BRCA1 (Ogita et al., 2018).
